posts.caption: The new boarder arrived Saturday with a brand new helmet, a very clean trailer, and a lot of questions. I walked her out to the paddock and made the mistake of leaving her alone with Big Red for ninety seconds. When I came back, the woman was standing in the exact spot Big Red had chosen for her, holding a lead rope she'd clearly been told to hold. Big Red had one hoof lifted and her eyes half closed. Nobody said a word. By Sunday afternoon the boarder knew where the good hay is kept, which gate sticks, and who runs the schedule.
posts.first: My first week at this barn, a gray mare decided where I stood for the next nine years. I was too new to argue and she was too sure. I still step to the left of the gate without thinking. Some lessons you don't need to be asked twice.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a huge copper-chestnut draft mare with white feathered legs, round glasses and gold earrings, one front hoof raised in a green pasture under a shade tree with a bucket of carrots nearby. Text at the top reads: The new boarder asked where to stand. I said behind me, in the shade, with the snacks.

posts.caption: The arena crew put out a single orange cone on Thursday morning, and Pudding has treated it like a visitor ever since. He walked the long way around it twice. Then he stopped three feet away and stared at it with his ears straight up, forelock flopping, like he was waiting for a name tag. It did not have one. I stood at the rail with a half-empty coffee and watched a pony hold a formal interview with a piece of plastic for eleven minutes. The cone is still in the arena. He has agreed to let it stay.
posts.first: I once spent twenty minutes on a trail because my mare refused to pass a stump. A stump, in full view, that had been there longer than either of us. I got off, walked her past it, and apologized to the stump. That's just how a Tuesday goes.

posts.theme: the horse budget vs. the spouse
posts.quote: The hay bill came in $212 over what I told my husband. I've filed the difference under 'weather.'
posts.first: The weather did drop below zero for a week, so it's not entirely untrue. I did the math at the kitchen table after he went to bed. At breakfast he asked how the hay was holding up. I said 'consistent.'

posts.caption: The nail by his stall door has been empty twice in nineteen years. Once for a move, and once when I lent the halter to a friend's daughter for a pony club photo. Both times I drove back in the dark to put it where it belongs. It's plain brown leather, cracked at the buckle, too small for his head now. Last Thursday I sat on the bucket with a rag and a tin of conditioner and worked on it for an hour. He stood next to me and breathed on my hair. Neither of us mentioned it.
posts.first: The halter cost forty dollars at a tack swap in a parking lot. The woman selling it said he'd grow into it. He did, and then he grew out. I've never found a better forty dollars. I'd tell you where, but it's a field now.

I let her think I didn't notice, and she let me think she wasn't crying.

posts.caption: The monthly spreadsheet went out last Sunday and my husband read it at the counter with his tea. Hay, shavings, farrier, one vet visit, a blanket I'd labeled a repair. He circled a number, then another, then put the pen down and looked out at the paddock. The Diva was standing at the fence in her good halter, tossing her mane for nobody. He sighed the sigh of a man who has lost a close argument to a horse. Then he refilled his tea and said the car could use new tires next month. We both knew they'd wait.
posts.first: The car is a 2011 hatchback with a cracked dash and a hay stain on the back seat that will outlive me. I drive it to the barn twice a day. I love it. It has just never once made me stop and stare at it over a stall door.

posts.caption: Sunday the clocks went back and the barn went dark at four-forty. I was out there with a headlamp doing evening feed in the blue light, and every horse looked at me like I'd personally ordered the night. Except one. The Homebody had already pulled the quilt down over her stall door and switched on her string lights, and she stood under them with the barn cat asleep on her back like a tiny tenant. I topped off her water and her mash, then stayed in the doorway longer than I needed to. It's warm in there. I didn't want to leave either.
posts.first: The string lights were a clearance find in January, three boxes for eleven dollars. I hung them in her stall as a joke. They've been up ever since. The cat sleeps under them in a coil of extension cord I keep meaning to move. I haven't.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a plump bay mare in a lavender fleece cooler lying in deep straw in a cozy stall with glowing string lights, a barn cat on her back and a dark evening window. Headline: Daylight saving ended. The barn is dark by five. Subtitle: I'm treating it as permission.
